U.S. rail traffic rose 4.7% for the week ending November 21 from a year ago, the Association of American Railroads said, as intermodal volume again drove gains.
Containers and trailers improved 8.3% compared with the same week in 2025, while commodity carloads edged up 0.5%.
(Chart: AAR)
Six of the 10 carload commodity groups posted gains. Metallic ores and metals used in steelmaking led at 17.9%. Forest products rose 11% despite real estate market issues; petroleum and petroleum products improved 11.2%, and motor vehicles and parts rose 8.3% as year-end sales promotions outweighed higher interest rates. Farm products excluding grain and food were up 6.2%, and chemicals increased 2.1%.
Four groups declined as grain fell 17.4%, the steepest drop. Coal was off 4.4%, while unspecified carloads were off 2.1%, and nonmetallic minerals such as sand and stone dropped 0.9%.
Through the first 46 weeks of 2026, total U.S. rail freight traffic is up 4% from last 2025. Carloads are better by 2.7% and intermodal units are up 5.1%. Among commodities, metallic ores and metals lead year-to-date at 9%, followed by grain at 8.7% and petroleum products at 7.9%. Coal is the only major group down year-to-date, at 1.6%.
Across nine reporting U.S., Canadian and Mexican railroads, North American carloads for the week slipped 0.3%, while intermodal was ahead 8.4%. Combined traffic gained by 4.2%. For the first 46 weeks of the year, combined North American volume is up 3.5% from 2025.
Why It Matters: Rail volumes point to uneven conditions. Strong intermodal growth, which is tied to consumer goods and retail logistics, suggests healthy import and holiday-season shipping demand. Gains in metals, autos and petroleum point to steady industrial activity, while weaker grain and coal volumes show agricultural and energy shipments may be softening.
